props.title: Hour of the Wolf
props.initialSlug: Artist's descent into madness haunts isolated island

sections.content: **Hour of the Wolf** (1968) marks Ingmar Bergman's only explicit venture into horror, blending psychological terror with his signature existential dread. The film follows artist Johan Borg (Max von Sydow) and his pregnant wife Alma (Liv Ullmann) on a remote island where reality dissolves into nightmare. Bergman's influence on psychological horror reverberates through films like **The Shining** (1980) and **Black Swan** (2010), particularly in their exploration of artistic madness and isolation. The film's surreal dinner party sequence directly inspired similar scenes in **Mother!** (2017) and **Eraserhead** (1977).

sections.content: The film's innovative sound design and use of silence created a template for psychological horror. The "hour of the wolf" - the time between night and dawn when most deaths occur - influenced countless horror films' use of the witching hour, from **The Exorcist** (1973) to **A Nightmare on Elm Street** (1984). Bergman's manipulation of reality versus hallucination particularly resonates in modern psychological thrillers like **Mulholland Drive** (2001) and **The Babadook** (2014).

The marriage dynamics in Hour of the Wolf echo through later horror films about relationships under supernatural strain. **Antichrist** (2009) directly references Bergman's work in its isolated couple facing psychological breakdown, while **The Others** (2001) adopts similar techniques in portraying a woman's isolation and uncertainty about reality. movies.slug: A grieving couple retreats to a cabin in the woods where psychological and supernatural horror merge.

sections.content: Contemporary filmmakers continue drawing from Hour of the Wolf's psychological horror playbook. **Midsommar** (2019) echoes its Scandinavian unease and relationship decay, while **The Lighthouse** (2019) directly channels its isolation-induced madness. Robert Eggers cited Hour of the Wolf as a primary influence, particularly in depicting the deteriorating psyche through increasingly surreal imagery.
